quartiers:Plaka.name: Plaka
quartiers:Plaka.teaser: The quarter the city never left, at its best before the first coach parks
quartiers:Plaka.story: Plaka is the piece of Athens that stayed lived in through every century the city shrank, pressed against the north-east flank of the Acropolis rock. Its streets stack the ages: Byzantine chapels sunk below today's pavement, Ottoman-era houses, neoclassical fronts from the new capital of the 1830s, and above them the whitewashed island lanes of Anafiotika. It is also the most visited square kilometre in Greece, and by mid-morning the marble steps are a queue. At eight it belongs to shopkeepers hosing their doorsteps, and a wet winter evening hands it back to the people who live there.
quartiers:Plaka.why: Walk it for the layers, not for dinner: the menus with photographs and the waiter on the pavement are the warning sign.

quartiers:Monastiraki.name: Monastiraki
quartiers:Monastiraki.teaser: A monastery, a mosque and Hadrian's library in one glance, and the flea market every Sunday
quartiers:Monastiraki.story: The square takes its name, the little monastery, from the Pantanassa church that still sits sunk in its middle, a monastic foundation usually dated to the tenth century. Turn round and the Tzistarakis mosque of 1759 faces you, and behind its shoulder runs the colonnaded wall of Hadrian's Library; the metro trains surface right beside the ancient stones. This was the bazaar crossroads of Ottoman Athens and it still trades like one. On Sunday morning the dealers spread brass, records, army surplus and family photographs across the square at Avissynias, and the haggling starts early.
quartiers:Monastiraki.why: Come on Sunday by 08:00, before the junk dealers' best pieces are carried off.

quartiers:Psyrri.name: Psyrri
quartiers:Psyrri.teaser: Hammers in the morning, bouzouki at night, and the walls painted in between
quartiers:Psyrri.story: Psyrri was the craftsmen's quarter: tinsmiths, leather cutters, sandal makers and basket weavers in low workshops round Plateia Iroon. In the 1990s the city pushed bars and clubs into the empty units and the name came to mean nightlife, but some of the benches never closed, and on a weekday morning you still hear metal being beaten into shape. The walls carry some of the most crowded street painting in the city. After dark the sound changes: rebetiko from cellar rooms on Friday and Saturday nights, and the dawn bakers lighting their ovens as the last tables empty.
quartiers:Psyrri.why: Do it twice: a weekday morning for the workshops, then a Saturday late for the music.

quartiers:Exarcheia.name: Exarcheia
quartiers:Exarcheia.teaser: The Polytechnic's quarter: radical presses, record shops and a square still under metro works
quartiers:Exarcheia.story: Exarcheia sits behind the Polytechnic, where students occupied the school in November 1973 until a tank broke down the gate, an uprising that helped bring down the junta within a year. The quarter has stayed political ever since, and it is where Greek publishing lives: small presses, used bookshops and record dealers on every block below Strefi Hill. Its square has been a building site since August 2022 for a Line 4 station, against loud local opposition. In 2026 the tunnelling stalled in neighbouring Kypseli after apartment blocks cracked, so expect the hoardings to stay.
quartiers:Exarcheia.why: Spend the morning in the bookshops and record stores, then sit somewhere with ouzo as the evening starts.

quartiers:Metaxourgeio / Kerameikos.name: Metaxourgeio and Kerameikos
quartiers:Metaxourgeio / Kerameikos.teaser: A silk mill gave it the name; galleries, wholesalers and an ancient cemetery share it now
quartiers:Metaxourgeio / Kerameikos.story: Metaxourgeio means silk works, after the nineteenth-century mill whose shell still stands on Avdi Square. The quarter went industrial, then red-light, then empty, and what moved in is a mix found nowhere else in the centre: Chinese wholesale shops, artist-run spaces, Rebecca Camhi's gallery (founded 1995), small theatres and late koutoukia. A few streets west lies the ancient Kerameikos, the potters' district and the city's cemetery, reopened in September 2026 after a long closure for works. On a summer night Avdi Square fills with people from the theatres and the bars and stays full past midnight.
quartiers:Metaxourgeio / Kerameikos.why: Come after 20:00 in summer, when Avdi Square is the living room of the whole quarter.

quartiers:Kolonaki.name: Kolonaki
quartiers:Kolonaki.teaser: Embassies, tailors and two great museums on the slope of Lycabettus; a salon, not a kitchen
quartiers:Kolonaki.story: Kolonaki means little column, and the quarter climbs from that modest marker up the flank of Lycabettus. It is the address of old Athenian money: embassies, tailors, gallery after gallery, and on its lower edge the Benaki and the Museum of Cycladic Art, both with their own cards. People come here to be seen with a coffee, not to eat well. Near the top, the plane trees of Dexameni shade the old literary kafeneio and, in summer, an open-air cinema where the films run under the pines of the hill.
quartiers:Kolonaki.why: Climb to Dexameni at aperitivo hour on a weekday, and stay for the open-air film in summer.

quartiers:Pangrati.name: Pangrati
quartiers:Pangrati.teaser: Behind the marble stadium, the residential quarter that cooks harder than any other in Athens
quartiers:Pangrati.story: Pangrati climbs behind the Kallimarmaro, the all-marble stadium of the 1896 Olympics, a middle-class grid of apartment blocks where the poet Seferis and the composer Hatzidakis both made their homes. Time Out put it 39th on its 2022 list of the world's coolest neighbourhoods, but the case for it is made at the table: more serious kitchens per street than anywhere in the city, from a Bib Gourmand open fire to a half-basement taverna that chefs use on their nights off. The evening runs between Plateia Proskopon and Plateia Varnava, starting with vermouth and ending late.
quartiers:Pangrati.why: Start with a vermouth on Varnava, then dinner booked ahead; Thursday to Saturday fills fast.

quartiers:Koukaki.name: Koukaki
quartiers:Koukaki.teaser: A working grid below Filopappou that short lets have hollowed out, its café streets still standing
quartiers:Koukaki.story: Koukaki is a grid of postwar blocks under Filopappou hill that became the city's short-let capital in a decade. A ProtoThema investigation in June 2025 estimated that 60 to 70 per cent of its long-term tenants had been pushed out, and on summer weekend nights it feels like a hotel corridor. In the morning it is still a neighbourhood: retirees at the kiosk, children heading to school, the café tables on Olympiou and Drakou filling with people who live here. The Acropolis Museum stands at its edge, and the prices in between have not caught up with Plaka's.
quartiers:Koukaki.why: Come on a weekday morning, when the coffee streets still belong to residents.
facts: Coffee on Olympiou and Drakou, and the quiet side of the Acropolis Museum

quartiers:Ano Petralona.name: Ano Petralona
quartiers:Ano Petralona.teaser: Bitter-orange trees, low pastel houses and the most honest tavernas in the centre
quartiers:Ano Petralona.story: Ano Petralona lies between the old electric railway and the western slope of Filopappou, and it is as close as the centre gets to a prewar village. The houses are low and painted, bitter-orange trees line the pavements, and the old ironwork balconies still hold pots of basil. People come for the tavernas: the densest run of plain, good ones in central Athens, along Troon and around Plateia Merkouri. On summer nights the tables cross the pavement and half the street eats outside; on Sunday the same tables fill at lunch with three generations at once.
quartiers:Ano Petralona.why: Book a pavement table on Troon for a summer night, or go at Sunday lunch to see the families.

quartiers:Kypseli.name: Kypseli
quartiers:Kypseli.teaser: Art Deco lobbies, Ghanaian barbers and new coffee bars along one long garden promenade
quartiers:Kypseli.story: Kypseli was built for the Athenian middle class from the 1930s into the 1960s, in apartment blocks with marble lobbies and Art Deco doors, and at its peak it was among the most densely populated districts in Europe. The middle class moved out to the suburbs, migrants from Africa and Asia moved in, and now younger Athenians are coming back. Its spine is Fokionos Negri, a planted promenade where barbershops, roasters and old pastry shops share the pavement, with the restored Municipal Market as its anchor. The Line 4 tunnelling here stopped in May 2026 after cracks appeared in nearby buildings.
quartiers:Kypseli.why: Join the early-evening stroll on Fokionos Negri, when the whole quarter comes outside.

walks:The Pikionis Paths of Philopappou.name: The Pikionis paths of Philopappou
walks:The Pikionis Paths of Philopappou.teaser: A path laid stone by stone from the rubble of old Athens, with the Parthenon framed at every turn
walks:The Pikionis Paths of Philopappou.story: Between 1954 and 1957 the architect Dimitris Pikionis, a professor at the Polytechnic, paved the approaches to the Acropolis and Filopappou hill without finished drawings. He gathered marble and clay from demolished neoclassical houses and set it on site with his students, one piece at a time, so that no stretch repeats. Fragments of door frames and old cornices still show among the slabs. Look up as you walk: the pines open and close on the Parthenon at angles he chose. In 1996 the Ministry of Culture listed the paths as a protected monument.
walks:The Pikionis Paths of Philopappou.why: Watch your feet as well as the view: the old marble turns slippery when wet and there is no water on top.
facts: Opposite the junction of Dionysiou Areopagitou and Apostolou Pavlou

walks:Dionysiou Areopagitou — the Grand.name: Dionysiou Areopagitou, the grand promenade
walks:Dionysiou Areopagitou — the Grand.teaser: A marble avenue along the whole south slope of the Acropolis, open to walkers since the 2000s
walks:Dionysiou Areopagitou — the Grand.story: Until the early 2000s cars parked along this road under the Acropolis. The Unification of Archaeological Sites programme closed it to traffic between 2001 and 2003, before the 2004 Olympics, and paved it into a single walk linking the Theatre of Dionysus, the Odeon of Herodes Atticus, Filopappou and the Agora. The street is named for Dionysius the Areopagite, the Athenian judge converted when Saint Paul preached on the Areopagus rock at its western end. The Odeon itself closed after the 2026 summer season for a restoration of about three years, so expect works on its arched front.
walks:Dionysiou Areopagitou — the Grand.why: Walk it at dusk and finish on the Areopagus rock as the floodlights come on.

walks:Anafiotika at Dawn.name: Anafiotika at dawn
walks:Anafiotika at Dawn.teaser: A cluster of island houses built by stonemasons from Anafi, high on the Acropolis rock
walks:Anafiotika at Dawn.story: Masons from the small Cycladic island of Anafi came to build King Otto's new capital in the 1840s, found nowhere to live and put up their own houses on the slope of the Acropolis. The story told in the quarter is that they used an Ottoman-era custom: a house roofed between sunset and sunrise could not be pulled down. Around 45 of those whitewashed houses survive and people still live in them, with blue doors, jasmine and cats on every step. The lanes are narrow, dead-end and double back on themselves, so you lose the city in five minutes.
walks:Anafiotika at Dawn.why: Go before the village wakes and keep your voice down: these are people's front doors.

walks:Kerameikos to Gazi.name: Kerameikos to Gazi
walks:Kerameikos to Gazi.teaser: The potters' cemetery, reopened in September 2026 after a long closure, then the gasworks 400 m away
walks:Kerameikos to Gazi.story: The word ceramic begins here, in the potters' quarter on the clay banks of the Eridanos, which was also the burial ground of Athens for more than a thousand years. Its great gate opened onto the Sacred Way to Eleusis. The site reopened on 15 September 2026 after a four-million-euro overhaul with a new visitor building on Ermou and a second exit on Agion Asomaton. The bulls and sphinxes over the tombs are casts; the originals are in the museum on site. Then walk 400 metres to Gazi, whose gasworks ran from 1857 to 1984 and reopened as Technopolis in 1999.
walks:Kerameikos to Gazi.why: Go in the last two hours before closing, when the light is low and the site is at its quietest.

walks:Kaisariani Monastery & the Hymettu.name: Kaisariani monastery and the Hymettus pines
walks:Kaisariani Monastery & the Hymettu.teaser: An eleventh-century monastery in a pine fold of Hymettus, half an hour from Syntagma
walks:Kaisariani Monastery & the Hymettu.story: Kaisariani has been holy ground for a long time. Tradition puts a shrine of Aphrodite at its spring; a Byzantine monastery went up here in the late eleventh century over an earlier church, and its monks kept vines and bees on the mountain until the house emptied in the nineteenth century. Hymettus honey was the yardstick of the ancient world, and the slope still smells of it: thyme and sage underfoot, bees in the courtyard, cold spring water from the fountain. Above the walls the replanted Kaisariani forest climbs to viewpoints over the whole city to the sea.
walks:Kaisariani Monastery & the Hymettu.why: Arrive early, before the heat, and walk up through the forest after the church.

walks:Athens Riviera: Flisvos to Edem.name: Athens Riviera, Flisvos to Edem
walks:Athens Riviera: Flisvos to Edem.teaser: Five flat kilometres of sea path, from a 1911 armoured cruiser to the yacht berths and the city beach
walks:Athens Riviera: Flisvos to Edem.story: The walk starts at the armoured cruiser Georgios Averof, named for the benefactor whose bequest paid about a third of her price. She led the Greek fleet at Elli in December 1912 and at Lemnos in January 1913, and has been a floating museum moored at Trocadero since 1984. From her gangway the seafront path runs without a break past Flisvos Marina, with berths for hulls up to 110 metres, through the seaside parks and on to the sand at Edem, where the tram stops at the beach. There is almost no shade between the parks.

calas:Edem Beach.name: Edem Beach
calas:Edem Beach.teaser: The tram stops at the sand: the city's own free swim
calas:Edem Beach.story: Edem is where Athens swims when it has an hour, not a day. The tram from Syntagma stops at the beach, and Palaio Faliro uses the sand like a square that happens to have water in it: families in the morning, people straight from work in the late afternoon. It is an official bathing beach, but the water is city water: fine to swim, without a Blue Flag and not as clear as the coves further south. That is the trade. It costs nothing, takes half an hour from the centre, and needs no car, no bus and no plan.
calas:Edem Beach.why: Take it for what it is: the quickest free swim from the centre, not the clearest water.

calas:Megalo Kavouri.name: Megalo Kavouri
calas:Megalo Kavouri.teaser: The best free sand within the hour, with a drowned road under the shallows
calas:Megalo Kavouri.story: Megalo Kavouri is about 900 metres of free sand with pines behind it, and it faces west, so the sun goes down over the water in front of you. The name means big crab. The municipality's own description points out the oddity: the remains of an old submerged road show through the shallows towards the islet off the point, and on a calm day people wade out along it. Families hold the shallow middle of the beach; the rocky ends belong to snorkellers watching fish among the stones. On summer weekends parking runs out by mid-morning.
calas:Megalo Kavouri.why: Stay for sunset: this is one of the few Attic beaches where it drops straight into the sea ahead of you.

calas:Akti Vouliagmenis.teaser: A ten-euro gate on a weekday, and Blue Flag water on a big, shallow, well-kept beach
calas:Akti Vouliagmenis.story: Akti Vouliagmenis is the sensible middle of the Riviera: a large organised beach with lifeguards, showers and a long shallow shelf that suits children. Go midweek, or in September, when the sea is at its warmest and the families have gone home.

calas:Astir Beach.name: Astir Beach
calas:Astir Beach.teaser: The priciest swim in Athens buys you history and seagull-wing shades, not clearer water
calas:Astir Beach.story: Astir opened in 1959 on old monastery land on the Laimos peninsula, and in its first decades Onassis, Bardot and Sinatra were on its sand; the seagull-wing sunshades from that era are still its emblem. The water is the same Saronic blue as the beaches either side.

calas:Limanakia (Cove B).name: Limanakia (Cove B)
calas:Limanakia (Cove B).teaser: No sand, no lifeguard, and the clearest water within 25 km of Syntagma
calas:Limanakia (Cove B).story: The Limanakia are a run of rocky inlets below the coast road beyond Vouliagmeni, with no sand, no lifeguards and no toilets; the only thing for sale is beer from a canteen. What you get instead is the clearest water near the city, reached by climbing down the rock and paid for in scraped knees. Since at least the 1970s these coves have been the city's free, bohemian shore, and cove B is Athens' best-known queer swimming spot, a fact the city's official tourism guide now celebrates. Off a red buoy lies the Devil's Well, an 11 m freediving hole with a real accident record.

calas:Lake Vouliagmeni.name: Lake Vouliagmeni
calas:Lake Vouliagmeni.teaser: A brackish lake in a fallen cave roof, warm enough to swim in January
calas:Lake Vouliagmeni.story: Lake Vouliagmeni fills the collapsed roof of a limestone cave under a cliff, fed by warm springs and linked underground to the sea, so the water is brackish and stays around 22 to 24 C all year. That makes it the one place near Athens where people swim in January without a wetsuit. Below the surface, cave divers are still mapping the flooded galleries that run back into the rock. In the shallows small fish come to nibble your feet, the fish pedicure the spas charge for. The free sea is 300 metres across the road.
calas:Lake Vouliagmeni.why: Come in winter: the warm water does its best work when the sea across the road is cold.

culture:Acropolis Museum.name: Acropolis Museum
culture:Acropolis Museum.teaser: The top floor turns 23 degrees off the grid so the frieze faces the temple 300 metres uphill
culture:Acropolis Museum.story: Bernard Tschumi's building opened in 2009 on more than a hundred concrete pillars, placed so as not to crush the early-Christian streets excavated beneath it, and you walk in over them on glass. Upstairs the logic flips: the top gallery is rotated 23 degrees off the rest of the building so the Parthenon frieze hangs in the temple's own orientation, with the real thing in the windows 300 metres away. Between 2011 and 2015 conservators laser-cleaned the five Caryatids in the open gallery while visitors watched. The sixth figure's place stands empty, kept for the one in London.
culture:Acropolis Museum.why: Climb straight to the glass top floor first, then work down; the frieze makes sense of everything below it.

culture:National Archaeological Museum.name: National Archaeological Museum
culture:National Archaeological Museum.teaser: Room 38 holds the oldest known geared machine, a bronze lump that turned out to predict eclipses
culture:National Archaeological Museum.story: Around Easter 1900, sponge divers from Symi sheltering off Antikythera found a Roman-era wreck about 50 metres down. Through the winter of 1900-01 the Navy hauled up bronzes and marbles, and among them came a corroded lump nobody could read. In 1902 it split and showed gear wheels: the Antikythera mechanism, an astronomical calculator of the 2nd to 1st century BC, with nothing comparable known for more than a thousand years afterwards. Every surviving fragment is in Room 38, ringed by the great bronze galleries, and the Mycenaean gold is quietest for whoever arrives at opening.
culture:National Archaeological Museum.why: Get to Room 38 before the groups do, and look at the gear teeth, not the reconstructions.

culture:Benaki Museum of Greek Culture.name: Benaki Museum of Greek Culture
culture:Benaki Museum of Greek Culture.teaser: One family's mansion holds Greece end to end, from the Bronze Age to 1922
culture:Benaki Museum of Greek Culture.story: In 1930 Antonis Benakis, heir to an Alexandrian cotton fortune and brother of the novelist Penelope Delta, gave the state his family's neoclassical house and everything he had collected. It opened in 1931 with Benakis as its unpaid director, and he went on buying, and asking friends for, objects until his death in 1954. The rooms run in order through the centuries, and the part people remember is the 18th-century carved and gilded reception rooms taken out of Kozani mansions and rebuilt whole, dim and complete. On Thursday evenings the permanent galleries are free and open late, and the roof café fills.

Chocolate suffers in an Athens August, so this is a cool-month errand, or one for the last stop before the tender.

around:Domaine Papagiannakos.name: Domaine Papagiannakos
around:Domaine Papagiannakos.teaser: Old-vine Savatiano and a modern retsina, poured in Greece's first bioclimatic winery on the Mesogeia plain
around:Domaine Papagiannakos.story: The Mesogeia plain east of Athens was the ancient city's vineyard, and Savatiano its workhorse grape, long blamed for bad retsina. The Papagiannakos family, bottling since 1919, set out to prove the grape wrong. In 2007 Vassilis Papagiannakos opened a gravity-fed winery outside Markopoulo that the family describes as the first bioclimatic winery in Greece, and from 50 to 60 year old dry-farmed vines he makes Savatiano with baked apple, fresh almond and a thyme-scrub salinity. The Retsina of Mesogaia, resinated lightly, is the bottle that changed minds about Attica's own wine.

around:Cape Sounion.name: Cape Sounion
around:Cape Sounion.teaser: White Doric columns on the last headland of Attica, where Byron cut his name and the day ends over the sea
around:Cape Sounion.story: At the southern tip of Attica the Temple of Poseidon stands on a cliff above the Aegean, built around 444 to 440 BC, in the same years and the same classical manner as the Parthenon. What survives is a row of white marble Doric columns that turn gold, then pink, as the sun drops into the sea to the west. Lord Byron came in 1810 and carved his name into the stone; you cannot walk inside the temple now, so look for it from the rope. He put the cape in The Isles of Greece: 'Place me on Sunium's marbled steep.'

bars:Tanini Agapi Mou.story: The name is a declaration: 'tannin, my love'. Since December 2018 this room on the quieter Neapoli side of Exarchia has kept around a hundred Greek wines, most from organic or biodynamic grapes, and about ninety of them are open by the glass, the deepest all-Greek pour in the city. Plants hang from the ceiling over birchwood tables by independent makers, and the staff wear no uniform. Culinary Backstreets called it 'the people's wine bar' in 2023, and chef Maria Kofitsa writes the small plates around whatever is in the glass. bars:Alexander's Bar.name: Alexander's Bar
bars:Alexander's Bar.teaser: A stirred drink under an 18th-century Alexander tapestry, in the hotel partisans once mined
bars:Alexander's Bar.story: Efstathios Lampsas, a palace cook of peasant birth, founded the Grande Bretagne in 1874 on an 800,000-drachma loan. In the war the building served as Greek headquarters, then German, then British, and at Christmas 1944 EAM partisans, Manolis Glezos among them, packed the sewers beneath it with dynamite, then called the operation off when they learned Winston Churchill had just checked in. The bar sits on the ground floor facing Parliament: wood, leather, a walk-in humidor next door and, above the bottles, an authentic 18th-century tapestry of Alexander victorious at Gaugamela. Behind the counter, one of the city's deepest brandy cellars.
bars:Alexander's Bar.why: On a windy night choose this room over any rooftop: no view, but the most civilised drink in town.

bars:Retsina — the revival bottle.name: Retsina — the revival bottle
bars:Retsina — the revival bottle.teaser: Pine resin, by law no more than one per cent, over the old Savatiano vines of the Mesogeia
bars:Retsina — the revival bottle.story: Retsina is the Attica native. Aleppo-pine resin goes into the must during fermentation, by law between 0.15 and 1 per cent, and the base is usually Savatiano, the drought-hardy grape of the Mesogeia plain about 30 km east of the city, where Markopoulo dates its wine records to 1831. Made with care, the pine reads as herb, not hardware. Domaine Papagiannakos of Markopoulo sets the modern benchmark; the Georgas family in Spata makes theirs natural and skin-contact; Kechris Tear of the Pine is the fine-dining bottle and Gaia Ritinitis Nobilis the easy way in. Drink it soon: airport and warehouse sprawl is eating the vineyards.

bars:Ouzo, tsipouro, tsikoudia.name: Ouzo, tsipouro, tsikoudia
bars:Ouzo, tsipouro, tsikoudia.teaser: Three clear spirits, three different animals: read the label before the karafaki arrives
bars:Ouzo, tsipouro, tsikoudia.story: Athens keeps its spirits straight, and so should you. Ouzo is neutral spirit redistilled with anise; it turns milk-white the moment ice or water hits, because anethole will not dissolve in water, and EU law reserves the name for Greece and Cyprus. Plomari and Barbayanni, both from Lesvos, are the bottles to know. Tsipouro is distilled from grape pomace, so it keeps the fruit, and comes with or without anise: Tsililis from Thessaly, Idoniko from Drama. Cretan tsikoudia, also called raki, is pomace spirit too, single-distilled and never flavoured with anise.

bars:The grapes nobody else grows.story: The same revival that rescued retsina runs through grapes almost no one else grows. Assyrtiko comes off the volcanic soils of Santorini, taut and mineral. Xinomavro, from Naoussa in the north, is the acid-black red of Greece, built to age. Malagousia had all but disappeared until the 1970s, when Vassilis Logothetis, a professor in Thessaloniki, pressed cuttings on his student Evangelos Gerovassiliou, who brought the grape back into bottles; it is now planted across the country, Attica included. The pleasure of drinking Greek in Athens is that all three sit on the same list.

listening:Markos Vamvakaris.teaser: A Syros stowaway vowed to learn the bouzouki in six months or cut off his hand. He kept the hand
listening:Markos Vamvakaris.story: Rebetiko, the Greek urban blues, took its classic shape after the 1922 refugee influx from Asia Minor; its harbour origins belong to the Piraeus guide. Markos Vamvakaris (1905–1972) left Syros at about twelve and worked from the bottom up: stevedore, coal carrier, the slaughterhouses, where he swore the vow. His first discs came in 1932, and around 1934 he formed the first bouzouki group to record and tour, with Batis, Delias and Pagioumtzis, moving the music out of the hash den and onto shellac. 'Frangosyriani', his 1935 song for a Catholic girl of Syros, became famous only in the early-1960s revival.

listening:Cloudy Sunday — Tsitsanis and.name: Cloudy Sunday — Tsitsanis and Bellou
listening:Cloudy Sunday — Tsitsanis and.teaser: Written under occupation, kept off record until 1948, and first sung with a defiant contralto
listening:Cloudy Sunday — Tsitsanis and.story: Vasilis Tsitsanis (1915–1984) wrote 'Synnefiasmeni Kyriaki' in occupied Thessaloniki in the shadow of the famine; the melody, he said, came out of the cloudy occupation. The studios were shut, so it reached shellac only in 1948, sung by Prodromos Tsaousakis with Sotiria Bellou. Bellou, born in 1921 near Chalkida, had arrived in wartime Athens with nothing, was heard by Tsitsanis, and from 1947 cut the 78s that made her rebetiko's defining contralto: flat, unornamented, refusing self-pity, and openly gay in 1940s Greece. Stelios Kazantzidis recorded the celebrated later version in 1959. Bellou died on 27 August 1997.

listening:1960 — the bouzouki at the Aca.teaser: In one year a bouzouki tune went to the Academy Awards and a Ritsos poem became national music
listening:1960 — the bouzouki at the Aca.story: Manos Hadjidakis wrote the theme for Melina Mercouri in Jules Dassin's 'Never on Sunday' (1960), and on 17 April 1961, at the 33rd Academy Awards, it won Best Original Song, the first winner from a foreign-language film; its harbour scenes are told in the Piraeus guide. The same year Mikis Theodorakis set Yannis Ritsos's 1936 poem 'Epitaphios', and two rival recordings came out within weeks: Hadjidakis's refined orchestration sung by Nana Mouskouri, and Theodorakis's laiko version, Grigoris Bithikotsis singing over Manolis Chiotis's bouzouki. The Bithikotsis reading founded entechno, the moment rebetiko's instrument became national art music.
listening:1960 — the bouzouki at the Aca.why: Hear both Epitaphios records back to back: the argument over Greek music is all there.
facts: Play the two 1960 Epitaphios recordings in a row: Mouskouri for Hadjidakis, Bithikotsis for Theodorakis

listening:Kapnikarea.name: Kapnikarea
listening:Kapnikarea.teaser: Unamplified rebetiko at table height in a Byzantine church's shadow, from mid-afternoon, all year
listening:Kapnikarea.story: In 1977 Sotiris Sofos, a tailor from Ikaria, set tables beside the Byzantine church of Kapnikarea. Ermou became a pedestrian street in 1996, and his son Dimitris has since let a rotating pool of about twenty-five musicians work the alley most afternoons from around 14:30: rebetiko without amplifiers, played at table height, with no stage and no set list. When the winter rooms go dark from June to September, this is the surest place in the centre to hear the music, and in daylight at that.
listening:Kapnikarea.why: Arrive just before half past two and let lunch run into the second hour of music.
facts: Christopoulou 2 at Ermou 57, beside the Kapnikarea church

listening:The winter rooms.name: The winter rooms
listening:The winter rooms.teaser: Two storied rebetiko rooms that play only in the cold months, neither yet confirmed for 2026–27
listening:The winter rooms.story: The rebetiko circuit's best-loved rooms are winter rooms, shut through the summer until October. In Ano Petralona, Giorgos Xintaris has held a Friday residency at Mousiki Skini Hamam, running October to May. In the Varvakios arcade, Stoa Athanaton on Sofokleous 17–19 was still singing in 2026, but under a shifting name. A search in October 2026 found no published 2026–27 programme for either, so treat both as a phone call, not a promise. If they answer, these are the nights to plan a week around; if not, Kapnikarea and Klimataria play all year.
listening:The winter rooms.why: Ring before Friday: a winter room that answers is worth rebuilding the whole evening around.
facts: Call from October; neither room's 2026–27 season was confirmed in October 2026

listening:Half Note Jazz Club.name: Half Note Jazz Club
listening:Half Note Jazz Club.teaser: Athens' serious jazz room for more than forty years, a Mets club that goes dark every summer
listening:Half Note Jazz Club.story: Half Note on Trivonianou in Mets has been the city's serious jazz room for more than four decades, the club the rest of the scene orbits. Its 2025–26 season brought the guitarist Gilad Hekselman and the Stavros Lantsias Octet. It closes every summer and for Easter week, so a July visitor misses it; in early summer the city's jazz moves outdoors instead, to the free Athens Jazz festival at Technopolis. In mid-October 2026 the new season's programme had not yet surfaced in search, so check the club's own listings before planning a night around it.
listening:Half Note Jazz Club.why: Choose the night by the artist, not the date: the booking is the whole point.
facts: Trivonianou 17, Mets, near the Panathenaic Stadium

listening:Lena Platonos — Gallop.name: Lena Platonos — Gallop
listening:Lena Platonos — Gallop.teaser: A 1985 record of analog synths, a drum machine and spoken poems that collectors now hunt
listening:Lena Platonos — Gallop.story: Lena Platonos made 'Gallop' in 1985 with analog synthesizers, a Roland TR-808 drum machine and her own surreal spoken poetry, and it sounded like nothing else in Greek music at the time. It found a second life in 2015, when the San Francisco label Dark Entries reissued it on vinyl, and international crate-diggers began to treat her as the Athenian name to hunt. Set beside the bouzouki story of this fold, it is the other Athens: private, electronic and strange, the city talking to itself late at night.
listening:Lena Platonos — Gallop.why: Play it after a night of rebetiko and hear how far one city travelled in a generation.
facts: The 2015 Dark Entries vinyl reissue; ask for it by name in the city's record shops

listening:Hi-fi — the one listening room.name: Hi-fi — the one listening room
listening:Hi-fi — the one listening room.teaser: One listening room this guide can vouch for, and an honest word about the rest
listening:Hi-fi — the one listening room.story: A listening bar is a room where the sound system and the records are the point and the drinks follow. This guide can stand behind one in Athens: the vinyl booth at Okupa in Kerameikos, which takes over from the laptops in the evening; its own card is under Rooms to linger & work. An October 2026 search turned up other names in online listings and a hi-fi showroom offering booked sessions, but none confirmed by the venue or the quality press for 2026, so none is recommended here. If you find one, judge it by ear.
listening:Hi-fi — the one listening room.why: Go to Okupa for the records; treat any other 'listening bar' as unproven until you have heard it.
facts: Okupa's vinyl sessions, Tuesday to Sunday evenings; its own card is in Rooms to linger & work
